chapter: Harlem, 52nd Street and the first big bands
title: Goodman and Benny Carter plan to go to Europe; Carter's arrangements in every book
summary: At the Park Central he, Goodman and Carter plotted moving to Europe; he describes how copyist Jack Mazel sold Benny Carter arrangements to other bands.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Gee, that's great. Who were playing at the other hotels in New York around that time?

Well, let's see, Benny Goodman was trying to have a band at Billy Rose's joint on 53rd Street there, which is now the Hammerstein Theater, and he was having a rough time. I remember I even gave him a couple of arrangements. And he and Benny Carter -- and I remember this as clearly as though it was right now. Were rather disgusted with the reception of jazz, you know, or of big band jazz particularly, and jazz in general, and we sat one time at a table there at the Park Central, plotting a European -- we were all going to go. Benny had just come back from there. And we -- and Coleman Hawkins was still over there, and we were seriously plotting to go to Europe and set up shop.

But nothing ever came of it because Benny you know, managed to get going and he -- well, you know, a lot of things are talked of that never happen. But I remember talking about it. Of course every band in New York that was any kind of a band at all had a Benny Carter arrangement in the book. He wrote more arrangements that he was not paid for, because he had a copyist by the name of Jack Mazel, or Meizel, and every time Benny would make an arrangement Jack would make an extra copy for himself. Jack's room was piled to the ceiling with Benny Carter arrangements, and other people's arrangements. And he would go around and sell the arrangements. And so any band at all that was playing arrangements, like Benny Carter's, "Take My Word," or, "Lonesome Nights," as it was originally called, and let's see, his, "Nagasaki," and his, "Devil's," something or other, oh, they were around in all the books.
Did Benny know how they were getting in all those books?
I'm sure he didn't. I think he just didn't care. He's such a nice man that he figured, well, if he's making a couple of bucks, what the heck, you know.
You'd think he might have changed copyists. Well, it's nice his work was so popular. He's a great writer.
Well, you weren't anything unless you had a couple of Benny Carter arrangements in the book.
